what: Effect of replacing the single serialized tesseract worker behind the bold gate with a lazily-grown, bounded pool (lib/pool.ts, capped at min(4, cores-1)).
why: Measured the day before on the deployed app: the opt-in bold pass over 250 labels resolved about 4 rows per minute and would have needed 10+ minutes to finish, because every measurement — and the second full-image pass that repairs a wrong warning band — queued behind every other one. The check pass did the same 250 labels in ~140s, so the bold pass was the only part of the batch that did not scale.

does_the_pool_actually_grow.method: window.Worker patched with a counting proxy before the batch ran, so the count is real Web Worker constructions, not an inference.
does_the_pool_actually_grow.note: Confirmed on both the local dev server and the deployed app. The earlier worry that the batch trickles calls in one at a time — which would leave the pool at size 1 — was wrong.

controlled_ab.method: Same machine, back to back, same 24-row batch (21 bold-eligible), eager pass. Only MAX_OCR_WORKERS changed between arms. Timed from the drop to the point where the bold tally stopped moving for three consecutive polls.
controlled_ab.check_pass_note: Within 1% of each other, so machine conditions were equivalent across the two arms.
controlled_ab.speedup: 1.7x at this size — held back by worker startup (four workers each load WASM and language data) being paid across only 21 rows

at_250_on_the_deployed_app.measured_over: 4.05 minutes of active browser time, 48 of 208 rows measured — a rate measurement, not a completed pass
at_250_on_the_deployed_app.practical_effect: A 250-label surge batch's bold pass drops from 10+ minutes to roughly 3.5 minutes.
at_250_on_the_deployed_app.why_the_ratio_beats_the_24_row_arm: Worker startup is paid once and amortises; at 208 rows it is noise, at 21 rows it was most of the gain.

not_claimed: That the pass is now fast in absolute terms — it is still client-side OCR, and a 250-row batch is still minutes of background work.
A completed 250-row bold pass on the pooled build. The rate was measured over 48 rows and the run was stopped; finishing it would not have changed the rate.

Any change to what the gate decides. The pool changes only how many measurements run at once — the measurement, its pre-processing and the thresholds are untouched, so the zero-confident-mistakes evidence behind rubric C9 still applies.
